title: Split a product into domains by capability
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a domain (A4) for each business capability of the product, before writing its records: Lathe's reference and its modeling skill steer each domain toward one capability, a vertical slice that owns its records, rules, views, code and tests, and away from technology layers such as the front end or the server. Each domain says its subdomain type, holds its capabilities in order with its use cases under them, and its glossary terms, domain services and repositories. `lathe check` warns of a domain named for a technology.

title: Change Lathe's schema with a migration
goal: The Owner adds a kind, a field or a relation to Lathe by writing the next numbered migration in `lathe/schema/`, and the change is reviewed in git like any other. `npm --prefix lathe run schema` regenerates the record types and `npm --prefix lathe run reference` the reference. The app and the aggregates' commands never change the schema. The loaded copy of the data is rebuilt from the data files on every load, so the next load checks every product's data against the changed schema. A change that existing data may not pass is breaking: it raises the schema version and brings the converter that moves products' data forward (LA-PLT-UC17).

title: Declare a product's own kinds and relations
goal: A product needs a kind or relation Lathe does not have. Without forking Lathe, the Owner or an Agent declares a product kind with its fields, and product relations, in any of the six stages, with the Product aggregate's commands, and writes records of the kind as extension records (A19), whose rules are their kind's declaration. Lathe generates a table for each kind and a link table for each new relation, with the same keys and rules as its own, and the next load accepts the product's records of the kind. Lathe's own kinds stay as they are.

title: Write a pattern with its rules
goal: Several use cases share the same behavior. The Owner, or an Agent, writes it once as a pattern (A2) under the product, with its named settings and its rules, each proved per domain by a pattern rule test; each use case or domain that follows it links it with `follows` and answers every setting, instead of restating its rules. The store refuses a setting name that is not lower case; `lathe check` reports a setting a follower has not answered.
notes: Lathe checks only how patterns are used, not house rules about them: a rule such as "each aggregate has exactly one use case following its Record view pattern" is the product's own check (LA-CHK-UC05).

title: Write a use case with its flow and tests
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a use case (A11) with its actors and requirements, its one flow, the same through every interface that offers it, as flow_step records on their paths, and its use case and flow tests: each step invokes at most one command or query, may exchange with integrations, fulfills requirements of its own use case, and names the one interface it is a variant of when only that one does it. Each interface's version of the flow is derived, never written. The store refuses a second flow, a flow ID that is not its use case's and FL, a repeated position or a requirement of another use case; `lathe check` reports a path that skips a number, a requirement the flow misses, a step an offering interface cannot reach and a variant of an interface that does not offer the use case.

title: Read each kind's stage and order from the schema
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, reads which stage each kind belongs to and its place in it, from the schema; a product places its own kinds in a stage; every list reads kinds in the schema's one order.

title: Model an aggregate with its entities and invariants
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes an aggregate (A6): its entities, at most one root and its child parts, each with fields typed by a basic type, a value object or a reference to another aggregate; parts linked by `has_one` and `has_many`; its invariants, each enforced by its own rule code and proved by its test, a uniqueness rule named on the unique key that enforces it; and each entity's data model. The app reads each entity's fields to draw a domain's ERD at aggregate level and each aggregate's own ERD.

title: Read the reference generated from the schema
goal: The owner, or an agent, reads how every kind, table, field, relation, stage and check works without opening the migrations or the checks: the reference script writes it from the schema and the checks, with a product's own kinds and checks, into `lathe/REFERENCE.md`, saying what clean architecture's use case is in Lathe (a command handler), and the API serves the same reference. Nothing in it is written by hand, so a new kind or check needs no edit, and the store refuses a product kind, relation or check that the reference would leave blank.

title: Model a command with its handler and policies
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each command of an aggregate (A8): the one aggregate it changes, the events it raises and the specifications it checks, its handler, and the policies under it that invoke it on hearing one event, each with its test.

title: Build a test data set
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a test data set (A17) under its domain: the starting records, environment and accounts some tests need, how to prepare and reset them, and the seed or fixture file that builds them with its aggregate's own commands. Tests link the data sets they start from; one nothing starts from, or whose file is missing, is reported.

title: Look up a kind or check
goal: The Reader meets a kind or a check while reading the spec (a record's kind in the wiki card, a problem's code, a field) and opens what the reference says about it in one step, without leaving the workbench. Each kind and each check has its own entry, built from the schema and the checks, so it is never out of date: a kind's stage, fields, links and checks with a real example from the product, and a check's explanation and query with the problems it reports now. The record format's own entry says how records are kept and indexes everything.

title: Write a standard with its rules
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a standard (A3) under the product, such as logging, error handling or naming, with a `standard_rule` record for each rule and the standard rule tests that prove it, such as a scan of the code for what the rule forbids. Each technical record that follows a rule links to it with `meets`. A reader finds the standards in the technical specification stage.

title: Specify a table and its keys
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a table (A18): where an entity's or read model's records, or a domain's links, are stored, its storage and its keys, a unique key naming the invariant it enforces, and the file that creates it; its stored fields follow from its record's fields.

title: Define a view with its requirements
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a view (A12): a place in an interface that presents commands and queries, with no owner, its product following from its ID, its address, the one interface that shows it when only one does, its view requirements and their tests. One that presents nothing is an error.

title: Merge two branches' data
goal: Two branches each change a product's data, an Agent's and the Owner's. When git merges them, the merge driver merges each data file record by record against the base, keeps both sides' records, sorts them again and checks the table's own rules, so that only a real clash stops the merge: one key added on both sides with different content, or one record changed on both sides.

title: Write a specification with its predicate
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a specification (A5): a named yes-or-no rule over one or more aggregates of one domain, reading the aggregates it judges, which commands check and queries select by, with the predicate that computes it and its test. One that nothing checks or selects by is an error.

title: Model a read model with its queries
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a read model (A10) under its domain with its fields, reading the aggregates it spans or fed by the events it hears; each query under the one read model it reads, with its handler; and the projection that builds it.

title: Write the business outcomes the product exists to achieve
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes the product's business outcomes first, each a measurable statement with its measure and target, and links each capability to the outcomes it serves, so the trace runs from why to proof.

title: Describe a product's roles and interfaces
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes the product itself (A1): the roles its use cases name as actors (Lathe's are Owner, Reader and Agent), its interfaces, each of a kind, with the roles that use it, the use cases it offers and the pattern it follows, and the open questions still to settle, each under the product or a domain and about the records it concerns. Each is written with the Product aggregate's own commands, which hold the product to its rules.

title: Define a value object with its constraints
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a value object (A9): a value with no identity, such as an email address, with its fields, the constraints checked when it is created and the value type that builds it. It has no owner and exists because entity, event or read model fields are typed by it; one that nothing uses is an error.

title: Model a domain event with its fields
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a domain event of an aggregate (A7): what happened, in the past tense, with the fields it carries and the event type that delivers it, published when other domains hear it, and delivered by outbox when a policy hears it.

title: Expose a command through an endpoint
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes an endpoint (A13) under the one command or query it exposes, titled by its method and address, with the API requirements it follows and the handler that serves it; a flow step reaches it only through its command or query.

title: Describe an integration with its adapter
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes an integration (A14): an outside system the product exchanges with, with no owner, its product following from its ID, the adapter that talks to it and its integration tests. One that no step exchanges with is an error.

title: Draw a view with a UI component
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes a UI component (A15) under its domain, naming its file, linking the views it renders and the view requirements its code builds. One that renders no view is an error.

title: Name a product's entry points
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each entry point (A20): a file that starts the product or one of its processes, such as the command line's bin or the desktop's main, named exactly as in code.

title: Name a product's tooling
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes the product's tooling (A21): the scripts and configuration that build, check and test it, each named exactly as in code, with the packages it uses.

title: Write a storage requirement with its tests
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes what the business needs kept of an aggregate or read model (A22): a storage requirement under it, stating what applies of durability, atomicity, retention and deletion, recovery and capacity, with the storage requirement tests that prove it at the level that can observe it. It is built once the aggregate's repository, or the read model's reader, names a file that exists and the data store it is kept in.

title: Name where a product's data lives
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, names each data store a product keeps data in (A23): a data server, a bucket, a folder of files, browser storage or memory, under the product or one of its domains, with the integration that reaches it when someone else runs it; then each repository, reader and table names the one it is kept in. A repository, reader or table that names none, and a data store nothing is kept in, are gaps.

title: Check the workspace
goal: After writing records or code, an Agent runs `npm --prefix lathe run check`, or the MCP `check` tool, to find out whether the data is broken and what work is left, and fixes errors before handing the work back to the Owner.

title: Add a check
goal: The Owner decides on a new rule, and an Agent adds it as a check so that every later load enforces it.

title: Add a product's own checks
goal: A product has house rules that Lathe should not impose on every product. One product, for example, requires each aggregate to have exactly one use case that follows its Record view pattern, and this repo requires every operation to state at least one API requirement. Lathe ships no such rule. Instead the Owner, or an Agent, adds each rule as a check of the product, in the same form as Lathe's own checks, with Add a check from any of Lathe's interfaces; it lives in the product's data. The check run applies them after Lathe's checks and reports their problems with the others, so the product's rules live and change with the product.

title: Keep each level of the spec a useful size
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, keeps each level of a product's spec small enough to read and big enough to group something. `lathe check` warns when a record holds more children of one kind than the product's `max_children` setting (`product_setting`), when an aggregate holds more entities than its `max_entities_per_aggregate` setting, and when a capability or a group holds only one record, counting a flow's steps per path and requirements and rules per group, so that a missing or needless level, or an aggregate that is several, is found while the spec is written.

title: Review every problem of a product
goal: The owner looks at everything the checks found in one product, on its space's own Checks panel, with the problems that belong to no product, to see what is broken before reviewing an agent's work.

title: Keep every change to the spec checked
goal: An Agent changes the spec only through Lathe's own tools and commands, so each change is one command of its aggregate, held to the aggregate's rules before it reaches a data file. A hand edit of a data file is refused before it happens, with a pointer to the tools, and the check then reports only the work still to do.

title: Find a record in a domain
goal: The reader opens a domain to find an invariant, a use case, a handler or a test, and to see what is missing.

title: Follow a record's links
goal: The reader reads one record and follows its links in either direction: from an obligation to the flow steps that fulfill it, the records that implement its design and the tests under it, or from a test back to its parent. To change a record the Owner edits it on its page (`LA-EXP-UC14`), or an Agent writes through the plugin; the page shows the change.

title: Walk the model as a graph
goal: The reader starts from any record, sees what it connects to, and walks the model by choosing one node after another, the way the record pages let them follow one link after another. The graph is one map of the whole model that never changes shape: walking it is zooming in and out and centering, so the shape of a domain and its traceability read at a glance.

title: Walk the graph through folder-like groups
goal: The reader reads the graph like a folder tree: the domain, then "Use cases (5)", then each use case. A record with many children shows one group per kind of child, so they see what is there and how much, and focus only the group they want to walk into.

title: Explore a record from several views at once
goal: The reader opens any record, group, domain or product at its one address and reads it two ways at once: its wiki page in the wiki card, and on the stage behind it among its neighbors (Graph), as an ERD on a domain, aggregate or entity, or as its traceability (Trace). Following a link in the card or a choice on the stage moves them both, and the header strip and the wiki card always name the record and its facts. They move around with a side navigation that folds away, find anything by ID or title, and read each page one level deep, opening only what they want.

title: Read a flow step by step
goal: The reader opens a flow and reads its steps in order, one line to a step, as a real product's flows read: what happens at each step, the command or query it invokes and the requirements it fulfills; on each interface's tab, where that interface carries the step out. They unfold a step to read more. In the graph the steps sit under their flow, and on a requirement's Trace stage they read the step that fulfills it.

title: Work in one product at a time
goal: The reader works on one product at a time, as in one workspace at a time in Slack, Discord, Linear or Notion. When the workspace shows two or more products, a rail at the far left of the nav shows each as a square icon; the reader chooses one and everything they see is that product's alone, as a separate space: the nav, quick find, its Checks, the wiki card, the graph and the ERD and Trace stages. They switch with Alt+1 to Alt+9 (⌥1 to ⌥9 on a Mac) or from the command palette, and come back to the page they left. With one product there is no rail, and the nav is that product's.

title: Read a product laid out in stage folders
goal: The reader reads a product laid out in stage folders, the way a real product keeps its specs. In the side nav, under the current space, Shared holds the patterns, the standards and the records with no owner; each domain folds into its five stages, then its open questions. The domain page and the group pages use the same folders and names as headings, so the page and the nav match.

title: Read the technical specification and test plan by kind
goal: The reader reads a domain's Technical specification and Test plan by kind instead of two long lists: the technical kinds, each under its own heading, and the ten test kinds in the plan's order, each test under the obligation it proves. The side nav, the domain page, the group pages, the graph and the header strip's breadcrumb all show the same groups.

title: Explore several places at once in tabs
goal: The Reader explores several places at once, as in a browser's tabs, and flips between them without losing their place. A tab is a place: its focus, stage, camera, depth, kind filters, wiki card and its own Back and Forward. Moving never leaves the tab, the same record may be open in several tabs, and a new tab opens only when the Reader asks for one: Cmd or Ctrl with a selection, or a middle press, on a box or a link, Open in New Tab, Cmd+Enter in quick open, Cmd+T or Duplicate Tab. The graph's layout, the minimap and the wiki card's width stay the session's whatever the tab. On the web the browser's own tabs are the tabs, each one place; in the app the tabs sit at the left of the page bar (on a narrow window, the Open pages sheet), the address and the window's Back and Forward follow the active one, and a reload brings them all back.

title: Read a domain and its aggregates as an ERD
goal: The reader switches to the ERD stage on a domain and reads its domain model as an entity-relationship diagram: its aggregates as boundaries around their entities, and how their entities' reference fields join them. On an aggregate they read its entities with their fields and relationships, and on an entity the same diagram with that entity picked out. The diagram draws entities and their relationships only. They choose a box to go to it, and read the key at the foot of the diagram for the boxes and the lines.

title: Look up a record's history
goal: The Reader wants to know how a record came to be as it is, without leaving the page. At the end of the expanded wiki card a History section, read only when they ask for it, lists the commits that changed the record's data, the changes not committed yet first, each with what it changed.

title: Read a domain's operations and integrations
goal: The reader opens a command or query and reads the operation that exposes it, with how it is called and its API requirements, opens an integration and reads the flow steps that exchange with its outside system, and finds operations in their domain's Interaction design and integrations in the product's Shared, as a real product's specs are laid out.

title: Watch the spec change
goal: As the product's data changes, by the Reader, by an Agent through any of Lathe's interfaces, or by a git pull, the Reader sees it on the stage in real time: live marks on the records added, changed and removed, Highlight changes, which makes every change obvious against a baseline (a New, Changed or Removed pill on each changed record, everything unchanged dimmed, a roll-up on every container, markers and hints for changes out of view), Next change and Previous change to walk them, the diff in the wiki card, a Changes panel listing the changes, and Follow, which glides the camera to each change as it lands.

title: Load the workspace
goal: Code such as the server's kept checks' run, or an agent's script, calls `loadWorkspace(root)` to get every record, link, problem and coverage figure for the repo at `root`.

title: Set up Lathe in a product repo
goal: Lathe is installed into a product's own repo as a package, so the product's data files live beside its code and Lathe's improvements arrive with a version bump instead of by copying.

title: See the current data
goal: While an Agent changes records with the aggregates' commands, the Reader keeps the browser open and expects it to show what is in the data files now, reloaded on the file watcher's Data files changed, and to say what is wrong when the data cannot be loaded.

title: Work the app from the keyboard
goal: The reader, used to VS Code and Claude Code, moves through the specs with the keys they already know: quick open, the command palette, toggling the panels and views, going back, jumping to problems, and a sheet that lists every shortcut.

title: See each command's shortcut where it is used
goal: The reader learns the shortcuts the way they are learned in VS Code and Linear: by seeing them where they already use them. A control's tooltip names it and its keys, the command palette shows each command's keys at the right of its entry, and assistive technology announces the keys too.

title: Arrange the workbench
goal: The reader sizes the navigation and the wiki card floating over the stage to suit what they are reading, as in VS Code: they drag a panel's edge, or focus it and use the keyboard, and the stage frames the focus again in what is left. Lathe remembers the sizes, and dragging the navigation small enough folds it to its rail.

title: Set how Lathe looks
goal: The reader picks how Lathe looks, as in VS Code: one of a few built-in themes (Lathe, High contrast, Workshop, Midnight and Graphite), and Light, Dark or the system's choice. They arrow through the themes and see each one at once. When none suits them, they duplicate one and change its colors, fonts, text size, density, corners, gaps and motion, with a warning wherever text gets hard to read, and share the result as a file. They choose, too, whether scroll zooms the stages or pans them, as in a map or a design tool.

title: Read the spec on a phone
goal: Away from a desk, the reader opens Lathe on a phone to read, not to arrange panels: they follow a record's links, check a domain's coverage, look at a graph or an ERD, and find a record by ID or title. One view fills the display at a time; the nav, the wiki card and quick find (and in a Product window, the open views) come up as sheets and go away again; everything answers a thumb, and nothing needs a hover. On a tablet in landscape they keep the Workbench, with targets sized for a finger. The decisions behind the design are in notes/mobile-design.md.

title: Read without anything jumping
goal: The Reader opens views, follows links, re-centers the graph, switches stages, collapses and resizes panels and folds entries, and the specs reload under them as they change. Whatever changes, what the Reader is looking at stays where it was: the panels hold still, new content takes the room kept for it, and anything that does move glides there on the shared motion. A header that grew with its title, a key that resized the diagram above it and a picture drawn once in the wrong place and then moved are the kind of jitter this rules out.

title: Use Lathe with a keyboard and assistive technology
goal: The Reader works without a mouse, or listens to the view through assistive technology, or both. They move through the nav, the tab panel, the wiki card and the stage with Tab and the arrow keys; open a record from the nav or quick find; switch stages; re-center the graph; fold entries; collapse and show the wiki card; and pick a theme. Every control says what it is and what it does in words that match what is drawn, every part that scrolls can be reached, nothing holds focus, focus lands where the Reader expects after each move and comes back to where it was when a dialog or a sheet closes, and what changes out of sight is announced. The Workbench reads as clearly in the High contrast theme, in light and dark, on a desk and on a phone. The findings behind the design are in notes/a11y-audit.md.

title: Open a product in a window
goal: The reader opens a product's folder, such as Lathe's own repo or another product's, and it opens in a window of its own with the product's name and folder in the title bar. Lathe in that window reads and live-reloads that folder, as in the browser. They come back to it from File › Open Recent, and the shell reopens the last folder when it starts.

title: Iterate on Lathe with hot reload
goal: The owner changes Lathe while using it in its own window. npm --prefix desktop run dev loads the Workbench with hot reload: from the owner's own dev server on port 5199 when it serves the opened folder, so the browser and the shell share it, or from a dev server of the shell's own. Changing the shell itself restarts it, and record changes reload the view in every mode. When they want Lathe as it ships, they build it locally, unsigned.

title: Use Lathe from the native menus
goal: The reader uses the menu bar as in any Mac app: File to open folders and close windows, Edit, View for the Workbench's views and the window's zoom and full-window mode, Window, and Help for the record format and the keyboard shortcuts. A menu choice runs the same command as its key in the Workbench.

title: Work under Lathe's own title bar
goal: The reader works in a window with no system title bar, as in VS Code: the window's controls float over Lathe's own bar, drawn in the theme's colors. From the bar they go back and forward, see which view they are on and open quick find, and show or hide the navigation. They drag the window by the bar and double-press it to zoom. When they change the theme or the light or dark mode, the bar and the window's controls follow.

title: Feel like a native Mac app
goal: The Owner keeps Lathe in the Dock like any well-made Mac app. Its icon reads at every size, in light and dark Docks, and a development build is marked DEV. The Dock badge counts the check errors of the space in front, and the Dock menu opens another product folder. About Lathe says which versions run, and Settings… opens the settings. From a record the Owner reveals the data file that holds its record in Finder, opens it in the editor or copies its ID, from the wiki card or from the context menu. Opening Lathe again, or a folder from Finder, goes to the running Lathe. A window opens calmly on the shell color, says which product it is opening, and, when the engine cannot load the folder, says why and offers a way on.

title: Accept writes only from the app
goal: The Owner changes a record in its aggregate's view, and the Workbench sends that one command's fields to its operation on the App server, which runs the command in its own transaction, the same command any of Lathe's interfaces run: it holds the aggregate to its rules, refuses it with every reason when it breaks one, and otherwise writes the aggregate's data files as a small diff for review in git. A request from another site is refused before any command runs.

title: Move a product to a new Lathe
goal: A product repo outside Lathe's own moves to a new Lathe safely: a Lathe reads only data for its own schema version, and lathe upgrade converts a product's data forward, one way, as one reviewable commit, listing what it could not convert. The Product window (LA-PLT-UC11) and the plugin (LA-PLT-UC18) use the product's own installed Lathe.

title: Start the plugin's tools in a product repo
goal: An Agent works on a product repo in Claude Code with Lathe's plugin. The plugin's launcher finds the repo and the Lathe installed in it and starts that Lathe's tools for the Agent, so the Agent writes through the product's own Lathe; when the plugin's skills were written for another major version of Lathe, the first tool result says so once, and the Agent knows its skills may not match the tools.

title: Work with Claude beside the stage
goal: The Owner works with Claude inside Lathe: in a chat panel floating beside the stage, their own Claude Code runs in the product folder, with their login, settings, skills, plugins, tool servers and CLAUDE.md, and the stage keeps framing the focus in the space the panel leaves. Claude's answers read as rich text whose record IDs open the record on the stage; its tool calls are compact entries that expand, the records it changed show as diffs, and a permission prompt waits for the Owner's answer in the chat. The Owner can stop a turn, resume, fork or start a session, and Claude can ask what the Reader is looking at and open a record in the window.
notes: Runs the user's own `claude` CLI headless with structured input and output (`-p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages --permission-prompt-tool stdio`, with `--resume <id>` and `--fork-session`); there is no API-key path and no agent loop of Lathe's own. Desktop only: the web app and a phone have no chat. Not yet: the CLI's interactive extras (slash-command dialogs, plan-mode approval, question cards); slash commands go to the CLI as text, and the panel's help lists what is not supported.

title: Talk to Claude
goal: The Owner talks to the desktop chat instead of typing: they dictate a message, its words appearing in the message box as they speak, and edit and send it; with voice activation on, "Lathe" after a pause opens the chat and starts the message, and spoken commands send, clear or edit it; with Quick mode on, the message sends by itself when they have finished. Speech is recognized on the Mac itself: no audio leaves it, and nothing is recorded or saved.
notes: macOS 26 or later only (SpeechAnalyzer); elsewhere the mic is hidden. It happens in the desktop app's chat (LA-PLT-UC19).

title: Review and undo Claude's changes
goal: After Claude has changed the spec in the chat, the Owner sees what it changed on the stage and decides: they put the turn's records under review, the stage lighting them alone while they step through each with its diff, follow a record ID in its answer into a new tab, or undo the whole turn in one step, which puts the records back through their aggregates' own commands or says why it cannot.
notes: It happens in the desktop app's chat (LA-PLT-UC19), after a turn that changed records.

title: Compose a message with more than words
goal: The Owner writes to Claude in the desktop chat with more than typed words: they point at records on the stage, type a slash for a skill, choose the model and effort, paste an image or send the stage as one, and send more while Claude works, each message waiting its turn.
notes: It happens in the desktop app's chat (LA-PLT-UC19); speaking a message is LA-PLT-UC20.

title: See a domain's coverage
goal: The Owner asks how complete a domain is: how many of its obligations (constraints, invariants, specifications, policies, domain services, UC requirements, view requirements, API requirements, pattern rules, standard rules and any obligation kind the product declares) are designed, built and proved, how many have only a test not automated yet, and which ones are not done. LA-TRC-UC02 says how each is decided.

title: Count coverage by the meta-model
goal: The Owner sees coverage for every kind of obligation the product has, its own kinds included. For each domain and obligation kind they see how many are designed, built, proved, and proved only by a test not automated yet, each decided from the tree: the steps and technical records that design and build it, and the tests under it.

title: Record how a test is run
goal: A person writes each test under the one record it proves, of the test kind for that record, and says how it runs in its run by: a level (unit, integration, service, system or browser, the lowest that can observe its result), a state (automated, manual or not automated yet), and a file, or for a manual test the reason it is manual. The store refuses a run by that breaks these rules; `lathe check` reports a test whose file is missing or does not name it.
notes: The store refuses a test without a state, or an automated test without a file; `lathe check` reports a test whose file is missing or does not back what it proves.

title: Prove the rules of the patterns a domain follows
goal: A pattern states behavior that several use cases share. Its rules are written once, as `pattern_rule` records under the pattern. Every domain that follows the pattern (the domain itself or one of its use cases `follows` it) owes every rule and must prove each in a pattern rule test of its own, naming the domain: proof in one domain says nothing about another. Pattern rules need proof only. A rule that holds for only some followers is not a pattern rule: it belongs to those use cases as their own requirement.
notes: The person writes the rules under the pattern, writes one pattern rule test per rule in each following domain, naming that domain, and runs `lathe check`. Coverage shows one pattern rule line per domain; the gaps and the `not-proved` warnings name the rule and the domain that still owes it. The store refuses a second test of one rule in one domain; a pattern nobody follows is reported.

title: Check that each test's file names it
goal: A test says what it proves by where it sits. A person, or an AI agent, writes the test and its code, and `lathe check` confirms that the code names the test, so each test record leads to the code that runs it.
notes: The person fixes each error by naming the test's ID in the test's name. A test whose file does not name it proves nothing: its obligation stays not proved, in the warnings and in coverage alike.

title: See each domain's tests by state
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, runs lathe check or reads the workspace's coverage and learns how many tests each domain has by state, automated, manual and not automated yet, as a real product's test-coverage summary counts them.

title: Follow a pattern per domain
goal: A real product adopts most of its patterns for a whole domain, writes several with no settings, and asks only for proof of their rules. The Owner, or an Agent, links a domain to a pattern with follows, and gives a pattern no settings where it has none. Coverage then counts each rule in that domain, as it does for a domain whose use cases follow the pattern, and asks only for proof. A use case that follows a pattern needs no requirements of its own. A product's own kind may be declared an obligation.

title: Report tests that count for nothing
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, runs `lathe check` and reads each pattern rule test whose domain does not owe its rule, with the reason, and each manual test whose file never mentions it.

title: See a product's coverage
goal: The reader opens a product to see its domains, how complete each one is (designed, built and proved), what is still undecided and what is broken.

title: Trace obligations from design to tests
goal: The Reader switches to the Trace stage and reads each use case of the product as one line, left to right: the business outcomes its capability serves, the use case, its design flows, their technical flow and its acceptance test suite, each stage with how far it has come (designed, built, proved). They open a line's stages down to its requirements, flows, steps, technical chain and tests, and select a requirement to light its path across the line, from the steps that fulfill it to the tests that prove it. Gaps show at once.

title: See every obligation kind and test state
goal: The Reader reads coverage for every kind of obligation the model names (UC requirements, view and API requirements, the domain model's rules and any kind the product adds), finds each view or API requirement under its view or operation, and tells at a glance which tests are automated, which are manual and which are not automated yet.

title: See a domain's owed pattern rules
goal: The Reader opens a domain and sees which patterns its use cases follow, and for each pattern rule, all of which the domain owes, whether the domain proves it, as a real product's "Patterns we follow" lists do. They open a pattern to see its settings, its rules and who follows it.

title: See tests by state with each domain's coverage
goal: The Reader reads a product's or a domain's coverage and, with each domain's coverage, its tests by state; the product's summary totals them, as a real product's test-coverage summary does.

title: Trace an obligation to its proof
goal: The Reader opens an obligation and, below its text, reads its Traceability: its chain as the engine works it out (what designs it, what builds it, each marked built or not, and the tests under it, each with its state), with a callout for each gap coverage finds. A use case's Traceability shows its requirements by Designed, Built and Proved; a technical record's, the obligations it builds and their tests; a test's, what it proves and its run by. Every list is titled by its links' label.

title: Check that addresses match the code both ways
goal: An operation or a view says where it is served by its address. A person, or an AI agent, writes the record and the code that serves it, and lathe check confirms both ways that they agree: the code of what implements each record names its address, and every address the code serves has a record. An address changed on one side and not the other, or served with no record, is found.
notes: The code is read as text, not run: an address built at run time, matched by a prefix, kept in a configuration file or given by a framework's file layout is not recognized as served. Name such an address in a comment of the file that serves it.

title: Check each stored record kind against the file that creates it
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, writes each kind of record kept in its own storage with the file that creates it: a migration, a schema or the code that makes it. lathe check reads that file and confirms it defines the stored kind as the spec says, by its name, its fields and its keys, so the spec and the real schema cannot drift apart unseen.
notes: The file is read as text, never run. What it recognizes, and what it does not compare, is in the check's explanation.

title: Account for every package the product depends on
goal: Every package a product's manifests list is there for a reason the spec names: a connector that calls it, an interface part that renders with it, a tooling record that runs it. lathe check reads the manifests and reports each package no technical record names, so a dependency never enters unexplained, and reports a record that names a package no manifest lists, so the claim never outlives the dependency.
notes: It reads each manifest as structured data, the four sections of package names alike: a dev dependency is tooling the product runs, so it is accounted for as a runtime one is. It does not read lock files, workspaces or other ecosystems' manifests, and it does not judge whether code imports a package: knip finds a dependency no code uses.

title: See the outcomes each record serves
goal: The Reader, or an Agent, opens any record and learns which business outcomes it serves, without anyone having typed the link in: the use cases that reach it say so. What no outcome reaches is reported, so it can be given the use case that needs it or removed.

title: Account for hand-written accidental complexity
goal: The Owner, or an Agent, records how each piece of accidental complexity is accounted for: a technical record written by hand fills a slot of a pattern, and a record decided outside the product names what provides it, so nothing accidental is left unexplained.
